name: Urinary tract infection
overview: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, bladder, ureters, and urethra. UTIs are one of the most common infections worldwide and are more prevalent in women than men due to differences in anatomy. The most common cause is bacteria entering the urinary tract through the urethra and multiplying in the bladder. Risk factors include sexual activity, certain types of birth control, urinary retention, kidney stones, diabetes, and a weakened immune system. UTIs can range from mild bladder infections to more serious kidney infections.
causes: Bacteria entering and multiplying in the urinary tract, most often the bladder.
typical_course: Typical symptoms of a lower UTI (bladder infection) include a strong, persistent urge to urinate, a burning sensation during urination, frequent urination of small amounts, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pelvic discomfort. If the infection spreads to the kidneys (upper UTI), symptoms may include fever, chills, back or side pain, nausea, and vomiting. The pattern of symptoms can help distinguish between lower and upper tract infections, with upper UTIs requiring more urgent medical attention.
self_care: General self-care guidance includes drinking plenty of water to help flush bacteria from the urinary system, urinating frequently and completely, wiping from front to back after using the toilet, and urinating after sexual activity. Avoiding irritants such as caffeine, alcohol, and spicy foods may help reduce bladder irritation. Cranberry products have been studied for their potential to reduce the risk of recurrent UTIs, though evidence is mixed.

diet.eat: Drink plenty of water (8-10 glasses daily). Include cranberry juice if tolerated. Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and spicy foods. Eat light, warm meals.

ayurvedic_lifestyle: Wipe front to back. Urinate after intercourse. Avoid holding urine for long periods. Wear breathable cotton underwear. Maintain good personal hygiene.
ayurvedic_caution: UTIs usually require antibiotic treatment. See a doctor for proper diagnosis and treatment. This is general wellness information only.

when_to_see_doctor: You should see a doctor if you experience symptoms of a UTI, especially if you have fever, back pain, or nausea, which may indicate a kidney infection. UTIs are diagnosed through urine tests and are typically treated with antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare provider. Prompt treatment is important to prevent the infection from spreading to the kidneys or causing complications.

name: Vertigo
overview: Vertigo is a sensation of spinning or movement, either of the individual or their surroundings, even when no actual movement is occurring. It is a symptom rather than a disease itself and can arise from various underlying conditions affecting the inner ear or the brain. The most common cause is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), which occurs when tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear become dislodged. Other causes include vestibular neuritis, Meniere's disease, labyrinthitis, migraines, and certain medications. Vertigo can range from mild and brief to severe and debilitating.
causes: A false sense of spinning, most commonly from a problem in the balance organs of the inner ear.
typical_course: Typical symptoms include a spinning or tilting sensation, loss of balance, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and difficulty focusing the eyes. Symptoms may be triggered or worsened by changes in head position, such as turning the head quickly, getting up from bed, or looking up. Episodes can last from seconds to minutes in BPPV, or longer in other conditions. Some individuals may also experience hearing changes, ringing in the ears, or a feeling of fullness in the ear, depending on the underlying cause.
self_care: General self-care guidance includes moving slowly and deliberately when changing positions, especially when getting up from lying or sitting. Avoiding sudden head movements and sleeping with the head slightly elevated may reduce symptom frequency. Staying hydrated and managing stress can also help. For BPPV, specific repositioning maneuvers performed under the guidance of a healthcare provider can be highly effective in resolving symptoms.

diet.eat: Eat light, warm meals. Avoid heavy, oily, and cold foods. Stay well hydrated. Include ginger in your diet. Avoid sudden head movements and lying flat after meals.

ayurvedic_lifestyle: Move slowly when changing positions. Practice gaze stabilization exercises. Ensure well-lit spaces. Avoid triggers like bright screens. Get adequate sleep. Manage stress.
ayurvedic_caution: Consult a neurologist for persistent or recurrent vertigo. This is general wellness information only.

when_to_see_doctor: You should see a doctor if vertigo is severe, persistent, or accompanied by hearing loss, severe headache, difficulty speaking, double vision, or numbness. These symptoms may indicate a more serious condition affecting the brain, such as a stroke or other neurological disorder. A healthcare provider can perform diagnostic tests to identify the cause and recommend appropriate treatment.
